entries.08a2f33ed78392d90696693c40f5db3bac6d9e42: <div sID="gen9029" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="5" osisID="Esth.5" sID="Esth.5"/> <div eID="gen9029" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9030" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen9031" type="x-p"/> The last news we had of Haman left him in his cups, <reference osisRef="Esth.3.15">ch. iii. 15</reference>. Our last news of queen Esther left her in tears, fasting and praying. Now this chapter brings in, I. Esther in her joys, smiled upon by the king and honoured with his company at her banquet of wine, <reference osisRef="Esth.5.1-Esth.5.8">ver. 1-8</reference>. II. Haman upon the fret, because he had not Mordecai's cap and knee, and with great indignation setting up a gallows for him, <reference osisRef="Esth.5.9-Esth.5.14">ver. 9-14</reference>. Thus those that sow in tears shall reap in joy, but the triumphing of the wicked is short.
entries.7eda1b7a23668d8884b9d55160ae52054b74e850: <div eID="gen9031" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen9030" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Esther's Approach to the King. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 510.)</title> <div sID="gen9032" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Now it came to pass on the third day, that Esther put on <hi type="italic">her</hi> royal <hi type="italic">apparel,</hi> and stood in the inner court of the king's house, over against the king's house: and the king sat upon his royal throne in the royal house, over against the gate of the house. <hi type="super">2</hi> And it was so, when the king saw Esther the queen standing in the court, <hi type="italic">that</hi> she obtained favour in his sight: and the king held out to Esther the golden sceptre that <hi type="italic">was</hi> in his hand. So Esther drew near, and touched the top of the sceptre. <hi type="super">3</hi> Then said the king unto her, What wilt thou, queen Esther? and what <hi type="italic">is</hi> thy request? it shall be even given thee to the half of the kingdom. <hi type="super">4</hi> And Esther answered, If <hi type="italic">it seem</hi> good unto the king, let the king and Haman come this day unto the banquet that I have prepared for him. <hi type="super">5</hi> Then the king said, Cause Haman to make haste, that he may do as Esther hath said. So the king and Haman came to the banquet that Esther had prepared. <hi type="super">6</hi> And the king said unto Esther at the banquet of wine, What <hi type="italic">is</hi> thy petition? and it shall be granted thee: and what <hi type="italic">is</hi> thy request? even to the half of the kingdom it shall be performed. <hi type="super">7</hi> Then answered Esther, and said, My petition and my request <hi type="italic">is;</hi> <hi type="super">8</hi> If I have found favour in the sight of the king, and if it please the king to grant my petition, and to perform my request, let the king and Haman come to the banquet that I shall prepare for them, and I will do to morrow as the king hath said. <div eID="gen9032" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9033" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. Esther's bold approach to the king, <reference osisRef="Esth.5.1">v. 1</reference>. When the time appointed for their fast was finished she lost no time, but on the third day, when the impression of her devotions were fresh upon her spirit, she addressed the king. When the heart is enlarged in communion with God it will be emboldened in doing and suffering for him. Some think that the three days' fast was only one whole day and two whole nights, in all which time they did not take any food at all, and that this is called <hi type="italic">three days,</hi> as Christ's lying in the grave so long is. This exposition is favoured by the consideration that on the third day the queen made her appearance at court. Resolutions which have difficulties and dangers to break though should be pursued without delay, lest they cool and slacken. <hi type="italic">What thou doest,</hi> which must be done boldly, <hi type="italic">do it quickly.</hi> Now she <hi type="italic">put on her royal apparel,</hi> that she might the better recommend herself to the king, and laid aside her fast-day clothes. She put on her fine clothes, not to please herself, but her husband; in her prayer, as we find in the Apocrypha (<reference osisRef="Esth.14.16">Esther xiv. 16</reference>), she thus appeals to God: <hi type="italic">Thou knowest, Lord, I abhor the sign of my high estate which is upon my head, in the days wherein I show myself, &c.</hi> Let hose whose rank obliges them to wear rich clothes learn hence to be dead to them, and not make them their adorning. She stood <hi type="italic">in the inner court over against the king,</hi> expecting her doom, between hope and fear. <div eID="gen9033" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9034" type="x-p"/> II. The favourable reception which the king gave her. When he <hi type="italic">saw her</hi> she <hi type="italic">obtained favour in his sight.</hi> The apocryphal author and Josephus say that she took two maids with her, on one of whom she leaned, while the other bore up her train,—that her countenance was cheerful and very amiable, but her heart was in anguish,—that the king, lifting up his countenance that shone with majesty, at first looked very fiercely upon her, whereupon she grew pale, and fainted, and bowed herself on the head of the maid that went by her; but then God changed the spirit of the king, and, in a fear, he leaped from his throne, took her in his arms till she came to herself, and comforted her with loving words. Here we are only told, <div eID="gen9034" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9035" type="x-p"/> 1. That he protected her from the law, and assured her of safety, by <hi type="italic">holding out to her the golden sceptre</hi> (<reference osisRef="Esth.5.2">v. 2</reference>), which she thankfully <hi type="italic">touched the top of,</hi> thereby presenting herself to him as a humble petitioner. Thus having had power with God and prevailed, like Jacob, she had power with men too. <hi type="italic">He that will lose his life</hi> for God shall <hi type="italic">save it,</hi> or find it in a better life. <div eID="gen9035" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9036" type="x-p"/> 2. That he encouraged her address (<reference osisRef="Esth.5.3">v. 3</reference>): <hi type="italic">What wilt thou, queen Esther, and what is thy request?</hi> So far was he from counting her an offender that he seemed glad to see her, and desirous to oblige her. He that had divorced one wife for not coming when she was sent for would not be severe to another for coming when she was not sent for. God can turn the hearts of men, of great men, of those that act most arbitrarily, which way he pleases towards us. Esther feared that she should perish, but was promised that she should have what she might ask for, though it were <hi type="italic">the half of the kingdom.</hi> Note, God in his providence often prevents the fears, and outdoes the hopes, of his people, especially when they venture in his cause. Let us from this story infer, as our Saviour does from the parable of the unjust judge, an encouragement to <hi type="italic">pray always</hi> to our God, <hi type="italic">and not faint,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.18.6-Luke.18.8">Luke xviii. 6-8</reference>. Hear what this haughty king says (<hi type="italic">What is thy petition, and what is thy request? It shall be granted thee</hi>), and say <hi type="italic">shall not God</hi> hear and answer the prayers of <hi type="italic">his own elect, that cry day and night to him?</hi> Esther came to a proud imperious man; we come to the God of love and grace. She was not called; we are: the Spirit says, <hi type="italic">Come,</hi> and the bride says, <hi type="italic">Come.</hi> She had a law against her; we have a promise, many a promise, in favour of us: <hi type="italic">Ask, and it shall be given you.</hi> She had no friend to introduce her, or intercede for her, while on the contrary he that was then the king's favourite was her enemy; but we have an advocate with the Father, in whom he is well pleased. <hi type="italic">Let us therefore come boldly to the throne of grace.</hi> <div eID="gen9036" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9037" type="x-p"/> 3. That all the request she had to make to him, at this time, was that he would please to come to a banquet which she had prepared for him, and bring Haman along with him, <reference osisRef="Esth.5.4-Esth.5.5">v. 4, 5</reference>. Hereby, (1.) She would intimate to him how much she valued his favour and company. Whatever she had to ask, she desired his favour above any thing, and would purchase it at any rate. (2.) She would try how he stood affected to her; for, if he should refuse this, it would be to no purpose as yet to present her other request. (3.) She would endeavour to bring him into a pleasant humour, and soften his spirit, that he might with the more tenderness receive the impressions of the complaint she had to make to him. (4.) She would please him, by making court to Haman his favourite, and inviting him to come whose company she knew he loved and whom she desired to have present when she made her complaint; for she would say nothing of him but what she durst say to his face. (5.) She hoped at the banquet of wine to have a fairer and more favourable opportunity of presenting her petition. Wisdom is profitable to direct how to manage some men that are hard to deal with, and to take them by the right handle. <div eID="gen9037" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9038" type="x-p"/> 4. That he readily came, and ordered Haman to come along with him (<reference osisRef="Esth.5.5">v. 5</reference>), which was an indication of the kindness he still retained for her; if he really designed the destruction of her and her people, he would not have accepted her banquet. There he renewed his kind enquiry (<hi type="italic">What is thy petition?</hi>) and his generous promise, that it should be granted, <hi type="italic">even to the half of the kingdom</hi> (<reference osisRef="Esth.5.6">v. 6</reference>), a proverbial expression, by which he assured her that he would deny her nothing in reason. Herod used it, <reference osisRef="Mark.6.23">Mark vi. 23</reference>. <div eID="gen9038" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9039" type="x-p"/> 5. That then Esther thought fit to ask no more than a promise that he would please to accept of another treat, the next day, in her apartment, and Haman with him (<reference osisRef="Esth.5.7-Esth.5.8">v. 7, 8</reference>), intimating to him that then she would let him know what her business was. This adjourning of the main petition may be attributed, (1.) To Esther's prudence; thus she hoped yet further to win upon him and ingratiate herself with him. Perhaps her heart failed her now when she was going to make her request, and she desired to take some further time for prayer, that God would give her <hi type="italic">a mouth and wisdom.</hi> The putting of it off thus, it is likely, she knew would be well taken as an expression of the great reverence she had for the king, and her unwillingness to be too pressing upon him. What is hastily asked is often as hastily denied; but what is asked with a pause deserves to be considered. (2.) To God's providence putting it into Esther's heart to delay her petition a day longer, she knew not why, but God did, that what was to happen in the night intervening between this and to-morrow might further her design and make way for her success, that Haman might arrive at the highest pitch of malice against Mordecai and might begin to <hi type="italic">fall before him.</hi> The Jews perhaps blamed Ester as dilatory, and some of them began to suspect her sincerity, or at least her zeal; but the event disproved their jealousy, and all was for the best.
entries.5fe6f560adc0060610581ce5da051df14045de08: <div eID="gen9039" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Haman's Joy and Chagrin; Haman's Mediated Revenge. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 510.)</title> <div sID="gen9040" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">9</hi> Then went Haman forth that day joyful and with a glad heart: but when Haman saw Mordecai in the king's gate, that he stood not up, nor moved for him, he was full of indignation against Mordecai. <hi type="super">10</hi> Nevertheless Haman refrained himself: and when he came home, he sent and called for his friends, and Zeresh his wife. <hi type="super">11</hi> And Haman told them of the glory of his riches, and the multitude of his children, and all <hi type="italic">the things</hi> wherein the king had promoted him, and how he had advanced him above the princes and servants of the king. <hi type="super">12</hi> Haman said moreover, Yea, Esther the queen did let no man come in with the king unto the banquet that she had prepared but myself; and to morrow am I invited unto her also with the king. <hi type="super">13</hi> Yet all this availeth me nothing, so long as I see Mordecai the Jew sitting at the king's gate. <hi type="super">14</hi> Then said Zeresh his wife and all his friends unto him, Let a gallows be made of fifty cubits high, and to morrow speak thou unto the king that Mordecai may be hanged thereon: then go thou in merrily with the king unto the banquet. And the thing pleased Haman; and he caused the gallows to be made. <div eID="gen9040" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9041" type="x-p"/> This account here given of Haman is a comment upon that of Solomon, <reference osisRef="Prov.21.24">Prov. xxi. 24</reference>. <hi type="italic">Proud and haughty scorner is his name that deals in proud wrath.</hi> Never did any man more answer that name than Haman, in whom pride and wrath had so much the ascendant. See him, <div eID="gen9041" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9042" type="x-p"/> I. Puffed up with the honour of being invited to Esther's feast. He was <hi type="italic">joyful and glad of heart</hi> at it, <reference osisRef="Esth.5.9">v. 9</reference>. Observe with what a high gust he speaks of it (<reference osisRef="Esth.5.12">v. 12</reference>), how he values himself upon it, and how near he thinks it brings him to the perfection of felicity, that Esther the queen did let no man come with the king to the banquet but his mighty self, and he thought it was because she was exceedingly charmed with his conversation that the next day she had invited him also to come with the king; none so fit as he to bear the king company. Note, Self-admirers and self-flatterers are really self-deceivers. Haman pleased himself with the fancy that the queen, by this repeated invitation, designed to honour him, whereas really she designed to accuse him, and, in calling him to the banquet, did but call him to the bar. What magnifying glasses do proud men look at their faces in! And how does the <hi type="italic">pride of their heart deceive them!</hi> <reference osisRef="Obad.1.3">Obad. 3</reference>. <div eID="gen9042" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9043" type="x-p"/> II. Vexing and fretting at the slight that Mordecai put upon him, and thereby made uneasy to himself and to all about him. 1. Mordecai was as determined as ever: <hi type="italic">He stood not up, nor moved for him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Esth.5.9">v. 9</reference>. What he did was from a principle of conscience, and therefore he persevered in it, and would not cringe to Haman, no, not when he had reason to fear him and Esther herself complimented him. He knew God could and would deliver him and his people from the rage of Haman, without any such mean and sneaking expedients to mollify him. Those that walk in holy sincerity may walk in holy security, and go on in their work, not fearing what man can do unto them. <hi type="italic">He that walks uprightly walks surely.</hi> 2. Haman can as ill bear it as ever; nay, the higher he is lifted up, the more impatient is he of contempt and the more enraged at it. (1.) It made his own spirit restless, and put him into a grievous agitation. He was <hi type="italic">full of indignation</hi> (<reference osisRef="Esth.5.9">v. 9</reference>) and yet <hi type="italic">refrained himself,</hi> <reference osisRef="Esth.5.10">v. 10</reference>. Gladly would he have drawn his sword and run Mordecai through for affronting him thus; but he hoped shortly to see him fall with all the Jews, and therefore with much ado prevailed with himself to forbear stabbing him. What a struggle had he in his own bosom between his anger, which required Mordecai's death immediately (<hi type="italic">O that I had of his flesh! I cannot be satisfied!</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.31.31">Job xxxi. 31</reference>), and his malice, which had determined to wait for the general massacre! Thus <hi type="italic">thorns and snares are in the way of the froward.</hi> (2.) It made all his enjoyments sapless. This little affront which he received from Mordecai was the dead fly which spoiled all his pot of precious ointment; he himself owned in the presence of his wife and friends, to the everlasting reproach of a proud and discontented mind, that he had no comfort in his estate, preferment, and family, as long as Mordecai lived and had a place <hi type="italic">in the king's gate,</hi> <reference osisRef="Esth.5.10-Esth.5.13">v. 10-13</reference>. He took notice of his own riches and honours, the numerousness of his family, and the high posts to which he was advanced, that he was the darling of the prince and the idol of the court; and <hi type="italic">yet all this avails him nothing</hi> as long as Mordecai is unhanged. Those that are disposed to be uneasy will never want something or other to be uneasy at; and proud men, though they have <hi type="italic">much</hi> to their mind, yet, if they have not <hi type="italic">all</hi> to their mind, it is as nothing to them. The thousandth part of what Haman had would serve to make a humble modest man as much of a happiness as he expects from this world; and yet Haman complained as passionately as if he had been sunk into the lowest degree of poverty and disgrace. <div eID="gen9043" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9044" type="x-p"/> III. Meditating revenge, and assisted therein by his wife and his friends, <reference osisRef="Esth.5.14">v. 14</reference>. They saw how gladly he would dispense with his own resolution of deferring the slaughter till the time determined by the lot, and therefore advised him to take an earnest and foretaste of the satisfaction he then expected in the speedy execution of Mordecai; let him have that to please him at the moment; and having, as he thought, made sure the destruction of all the Jews, at the time appointed, he will not think scorn, for the present, to lay hands on Mordecai alone. 1. For the pleasing of his fancy they advise him to get <hi type="italic">a gallows ready,</hi> and have it set up before his own door, that, as soon as ever he could get the warrant signed, there might be no delay of the execution; he would not need so much as to stay the making of the gallows. This is very agreeable to Haman, who has the gallows made and fixed immediately; it must be fifty cubits high, or as near that as might be, for the greater disgrace of Mordecai and to make him a spectacle to every one that passed by; and it must be before Haman's door, that all men might take notice it was to the idol of his revenge that Mordecai was sacrificed and that he might feed his eyes with the sight. 2. For the gaining of his point they advise him to go early in the morning to the king, and get an order from him for the hanging of Mordecai, which, they doubted not, would be readily granted to one who was so much the king's favourite and who had so easily obtained an edict for the destruction of the whole nation of the Jews. There needed no feigned suggestion; it was enough if he let the king know that Mordecai, in contempt of the king's command, refused to reverence him. And now we leave Haman to go to bed, pleased with the thoughts of seeing Mordecai hanged the next day, and then going merrily to the banquet, and not dreaming of handselling his own gallows.  <chapter eID="Esth.5"/> <div eID="gen9044" type="x-p"/>

entries.101830263be2b06946686098105d86bcf3a618d8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4424"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 5</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Esth.5.1-Esth.5.14">Es 5:1-14</reference>. Esther Invites the King and Haman to a Banquet.</title> <div sID="gen6399" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4424"/><hi type="bold">1. Esther put on her royal apparel--</hi>It was not only natural, but, on such occasions, highly proper and expedient, that the queen should decorate herself in a style becoming her exalted station. On ordinary occasions she might reasonably set off her charms to as much advantage as possible; but, on the present occasion, as she was desirous to secure the favor of one who sustained the twofold character of her husband and her sovereign, public as well as private considerations--a regard to her personal safety, no less than the preservation of her doomed countrymen--urged upon her the propriety of using every legitimate means of recommending herself to the favorable notice of Ahasuerus.<div eID="gen6399" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6400" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the king sat upon his royal throne in the royal house, over against the gate of the house--</hi>The palace of this Persian king seems to have been built, like many more of the same quality and description, with an advanced cloister, over against the gate, made in the fashion of a large penthouse, supported only by one or two contiguous pillars in the front, or else in the center. In such open structures as these, in the midst of their guards and counsellors, are the bashaws, kadis, and other great officers, accustomed to distribute justice, and transact the public affairs of the provinces [Shaw, Travels]. In such a situation the Persian king was seated. The seat he occupied was not a throne, according to our ideas of one, but simply a chair, and so high that it required a footstool. It was made of gold, or, at least, inlaid with that metal, and covered with splendid tapestry, and no one save the king might sit down on it under pain of death. It is often found pictured on the Persepolitan monuments, and always of the same fashion. <div eID="gen6400" type="x-p"/>
entries.f564eb5b7e9ef09f397ce03539b197e156a514ca: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4425"/><div sID="gen6401" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4425"/><hi type="bold">2. the king held out to Esther the golden sceptre that was in his hand--</hi>This golden scepter receives an interesting illustration from the sculptured monuments of Persia and Assyria. In the bas-reliefs of Persepolis, copied by Sir Robert Ker Porter, we see King Darius enthroned in the midst of his court, and walking abroad in equal state; in either case he carries in his right hand a slender rod or wand, about equal in length to his own height, ornamented with a small knob at the summit. In the Assyrian alabasters, those found at Nimroud as well as those from Khorsabad, "the great king" is furnished with the same appendage of royalty, a slender rod, but destitute of any knob or ornament. On the Khorsabad reliefs the rod is painted red, doubtless to represent gold; proving that "the golden sceptre" was a simple wand of that precious metal, commonly held in the right hand, with one end resting on the ground, and that whether the king was sitting or walking. "The gold sceptre" has received little alteration or modification since ancient times [Goss]. It was extended to Esther as a token not only that her intrusion was pardoned, but that her visit was welcome, and a favorable reception given to the suit she had come to prefer.<div eID="gen6401" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6402" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">touched the top of the sceptre--</hi>This was the usual way of acknowledging the royal condescension, and at the same time expressing reverence and submission to the august majesty of the king. <div eID="gen6402" type="x-p"/>
entries.28f5aebce79d0c8f2521974b869ea426ae91090a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4426"/><div sID="gen6403" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4426"/><hi type="bold">3. it shall be even given thee to the half of the kingdom--</hi>This mode of speaking originated in the Persian custom of appropriating for the maintenance of great men, or royal favorites, one city for his bread, another for his wine, a third for his clothes, &c., so that the phrase denoted great liberality. <div eID="gen6403" type="x-p"/>
entries.c48d154ed3623e5e1218029f66cc90b63af063ac: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4427"/><div sID="gen6404" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4427"/><hi type="bold">4. let the king and Haman come this day unto the banquet that I have prepared for him--</hi>There was great address in this procedure of Esther's; for, by showing such high respect to the king's favorite, she would the better insinuate herself into the royal affections; and gain a more suitable opportunity of making known her request. <div eID="gen6404" type="x-p"/>
entries.49c7facfb5f5c14f10d5f1225f2fd5af6354ad0b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4428"/><div sID="gen6405" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4428"/><hi type="bold">8. let the king and Haman come to the banquet that I shall prepare--</hi>The king ate alone, and his guests in an adjoining hall; but they were admitted to sit with him at wine. Haman being the only invited guest with the king and queen, it was natural that he should have been elated with the honor. <chapter eID="Esth.5"/>

entries.89bb335d7dae7b4c81bb9bad8faada97ecd65fbe: <div eID="gen15540" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen15541" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen15542" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen15542" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen15541" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen15543" type="x-p"/> Esther presents herself before the king, and finds favor in his sight, <reference osisRef="Est.5.1">Est 5:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Est.5.2">Est 5:2</reference>. He asks what her request is, and promises to grant it, <reference osisRef="Est.5.3">Est 5:3</reference>. She invites him and Haman to a banquet, which they accept, <reference osisRef="Est.5.4">Est 5:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Est.5.5">Est 5:5</reference>. He then desires to know her request; and she promises to make it known on the morrow, if they will again come to her banquet, <reference osisRef="Est.5.6-Est.5.8">Est 5:6-8</reference>. Haman, though overjoyed at the manner in which he was received by the queen, is indignant at the indifference with which he is treated by Mordecai, <reference osisRef="Est.5.9">Est 5:9</reference>. He goes home, and complains of this conduct to his friends, and his wife Zeresh, <reference osisRef="Est.5.10-Est.5.13">Est 5:10-13</reference>. They counsel him to make a gallows of fifty cubits high, and to request the king that Mordecai may be hanged on it, which they take for granted the king will not refuse; and the gallows is made accordingly, <reference osisRef="Est.5.14">Est 5:14</reference>. <div eID="gen15543" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15544" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen15544" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15545" type="x-p"/> On the third day - Most probably the third day of the fast which she has prescribed to Mordecai and the Jews.
entries.57b551605868831d35a0fad878d89b02cad9a3ae: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen15545" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15546" type="x-p"/> She obtained favor in his sight - The Septuagint represents "the king as being at first greatly enraged when he saw Esther, because she had dared to appear before him unveiled, and she, perceiving this, was so terrified that she fainted away; on which the king, touched with tenderness, sprung from his throne, took her up in his arms, laid the golden scepter on her neck, and spoke to her in the most endearing manner." This is more circumstantial than the Hebrew, but is not contrary to it. <div eID="gen15546" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15547" type="x-p"/> The golden scepter that was in his hand - That the kings of Persia did wear a golden scepter, we have the following proof in Xenophon: Ὁτι ου τοδε το χρυσουν σκηπτρον το την βασιλειαν διασωξον εστιν, αλλ' πιστοι φιλοι σκηπτρον βασιλευσιν αληθεστατον και ασφαλεστατον. See Cyrop., lib. viii., p. 139, edit. Steph. 1581. It is not, said Cyrus to his son Cambyses, the Golden Sceptre that saves the kingdom; faithful friends are the truest and safest scepter of the empire.
entries.907079445a18026b820d43119b8381473f45fd33: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen15547" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15548" type="x-p"/> Let the king and Haman come this day unto the banquet - It was necessary to invite Haman to prevent his suspicion, and that he might not take any hasty step which might have prevented the execution of the great design.
entries.d5fe6415feb62a4d446963ae95857f2f619c93c0: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen15548" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15549" type="x-p"/> The banquet of wine - At that part of the banquet when the wine was introduced.
entries.b706519eb7c2851feb67b4a65a23aa75f513f330: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen15549" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15550" type="x-p"/> I will do to-morrow - She saw she was gaining on the king's affections; but she was not yet sufficiently confident; and therefore wished another interview, that she might ingratiate herself more fully in the king's favor, and thus secure the success of her design. But Providence disposed of things thus, to give time for the important event mentioned in the succeeding chapter.
entries.2931076601a294dad25d1290cc096191a15f2627: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen15550" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15551" type="x-p"/> That he stood not up, nor moved for him - This was certainly carrying his integrity or inflexibility to the highest pitch. But still we are left to conjecture that some reverence was required, which Mordecai could not conscientiously pay.
entries.3e61873931d5d4328bfdf9e58286cfc49557c3be: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen15551" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15552" type="x-p"/> The multitude of his children - The Asiatic sovereigns delight in the number of their children; and this is one cause why they take so many wives and concubines.
entries.67b0e44e74d6a3f84c0fd0ef761c13642f9ebde7: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen15552" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15553" type="x-p"/> Yet all this availeth me nothing - Pride will ever render its possessor unhappy. He has such a high opinion of his own worth, that he conceives himself defrauded by every one who does not pay him all the respect and homage which he conceives to be his due. <div eID="gen15553" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15554" type="x-p"/> The soul was made for God, and nothing but God can fill it and make it happy. Angels could not be happy in glory, when they had cast off their allegiance to their Maker. As soon as his heart had departed from God, Adam would needs go to the forbidden fruit, to satisfy a desire which was only an indication of his having been unfaithful to his God. Solomon, in all his glory, possessing every thing heart could wish, found all to be vanity and vexation of spirit; because his soul had not God for its portion. Ahab, on the throne of Israel, takes to his bed, and refuses to eat bread, not merely because he cannot get the vineyard of Naboth, but because he had not God in his heart, who could alone satisfy its desires. Haman, on the same ground, though the prime favourite of the king, is wretched because he cannot have a bow from that man whom his heart even despised. O, how distressing are the inquietudes of vanity. And how wretched is the man who has not the God of Jacob for his help, and in whose heart Christ dwells not by faith!
entries.93b33691a5e8e6169320a568998128f7a62efe82: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen15554" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15555" type="x-p"/> Let a gallows be made of fifty cubits high - The word עץ ets, which we translate gallows, signifies simply wood, a tree, or pole; and this was to be seventy-five feet high, that he might suffer the greater ignominy, and be a more public spectacle. I believe impaling is here also meant. See the note, <reference osisRef="Est.2.23">Est 2:23</reference> (note). <div eID="gen15555" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15556" type="x-p"/> In former times the Jews were accustomed to burn Haman in effigy; and with him a wooden cross, which they pretended to be in memory of that which he had erected for the suspension of Mordecai; but which was, in fact, to deride the Christian religion. The emperors, Justinian and Theodosius, abolished it by their edicts; and the practice has ceased from that time, though the principle from which it sprang still exists, with the same virulence against Christianity and its glorious Author.  <chapter eID="Esth.5"/> <div eID="gen15556" type="x-p"/>

entries.44c7ca9cebcdac28d712f0e0a47889b92907eb2a: <reference osisRef="Esth.5.1">Est 5:1</reference> <div eID="gen6750" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6751" type="x-p"/> On the third day Esther put on her royal apparel and entered the inner court of the king’s house, opposite the dwelling of the king, where he was sitting on his throne before the gate (<reference osisRef="Esth.5.1">Est 5:1</reference>). The third day must be counted from the day of the transaction between the queen and Mordochai (<reference osisRef="Esth.4.14">Est 4:14</reference>); the first day being that on which it took place. The fasting, then, would not begin till midday; and on the third day Esther went to the king to invite him on that day to a banquet, which would surely take place in the forenoon. Thus the three days’ fast would last from the afternoon of the first to the forenoon of the third day, i.e., from 40 to 45 hours. מלכוּת תּלבּשׁ, she put on royalty, royal dignity, i.e., arrayed herself in royal apparel. Bertheau thinks that the word לבוּשׁ has been inadvertently omitted before מלכוּת; but such a conjecture is without sufficient support, the passages <reference osisRef="Esth.6.8">Est 6:8</reference> and <reference osisRef="Esth.8.15">Est 8:15</reference> being of another kind. The expression is elliptical, and מלכוּת is easily completed by the notion לבוּשׁ furnished by the verb.
entries.0ca67ab8110c44f4bab2b36599295304f5279c01: <reference osisRef="Esth.5.2">Est 5:2</reference> <div eID="gen6751" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6752" type="x-p"/> When the king saw Queen Esther standing in the court, she obtained favour in his eyes (see rem. on <reference osisRef="Esth.2.9">Est 2:9</reference>), and he held out to her the golden sceptre that was in his hand; and Esther drew near and touched the top of the sceptre, probably kissed it, as the <hi type="italic">Vulgate</hi> renders the word.
entries.91edf496793122a6a0b68fc0b0150e8d49e63f4b: <reference osisRef="Esth.5.3-Esth.5.4">Est 5:3-4</reference> <div eID="gen6752" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6753" type="x-p"/> The king, concluding from the circumstance of her appearing there unsummoned, that she had some urgent matter to bring before him, said to her: “What wilt thou, Queen Esther? and what is thy request? To the half of the kingdom it shall be granted thee.” A short expression for: if thy request relates even to the half of the kingdom, it shall be granted. Est 5:4. Esther, however, for the present requested nothing further, than that on that day (to-day) the king and Haman should come to the banquet she had prepared. על טּוב אם like Est 1:19.
entries.49746b0ee5382c6e3efc29acdcab8d54dd66a9bd: <reference osisRef="Esth.5.5">Est 5:5</reference> <div eID="gen6753" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6754" type="x-p"/> The king commanded Haman to hasten thither, to do as the queen had said. מהרוּ, hastened Haman, i.e., sent to fetch him quickly. מהר like <reference osisRef="2Chr.18.8">2Ch 18:8</reference>; 1Ki 22:9. לעשׂות, that the word of the queen might be done, carried out.
entries.55b1df9e063980504fb79151cc2cd0be698f8785: <reference osisRef="Esth.5.6">Est 5:6</reference> <div eID="gen6754" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6755" type="x-p"/> At the repast, and indeed at “the banquet of wine,” when the greatest cheerfulness would prevail, the king repeated his question as to the desire of the queen, making the same promise as in Est 5:3. ותעשׂ, an abbreviated form of the imperfect תּעשׂה, is optative or jussive: and it shall be done.
entries.47d6315c88bd8ef606cc14a9e49e506936ef1112: <reference osisRef="Esth.5.7-Esth.5.8">Est 5:7-8</reference> <div eID="gen6755" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6756" type="x-p"/> Esther answered: “My petition and my request - if I have found favour in the sight of the king, and if it please the king to grant my petition and to do my request, let the king and Haman come to the banquet that I shall prepare for them, and to-morrow I will do as the king hath said,” i.e., make known my request. Though the king had, in the midst of the gaiety, asked what was Esther’s request, she did not esteem the time an appropriate one for expressing it. She begins: my petition and my request, - but then stops, and says only, if the king will do her the favour to come with Haman to a banquet again on the morrow, she will then bring forward her petition. Esther invited Haman with the king on both occasions, that, as Calovius remarks, <hi type="italic">eum apud regem praesentem accusaret decreti surrepti contra suos populares nomine, et in os omnes cavillandi vias ei praecluderet.  </hi>
entries.31d549977f345780477c71f7ef05a06f09db3dfa: <reference osisRef="Esth.5.9">Est 5:9</reference> <div eID="gen6756" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6757" type="x-p"/> Haman went forth from the palace satisfied and with a joyful heart. When, however, he saw Mordochai in the king’s gate, who neither stood up nor trembled before him, he was full of indignation against him. וגו קם ולא are circumstantial clauses following the principal clause without a copula. קם and זע are perfects, and ולא - ולא are used in the sense of neque - neque. זוּע constructed with מן means to tremble before any one, to be disquieted.
entries.3873a0c733a8647060226361e2e46f526eeb3cb7: <reference osisRef="Esth.5.10">Est 5:10</reference> <div eID="gen6757" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6758" type="x-p"/> Haman, however, refrained himself; and without immediately giving vent to his rage at Mordochai, went home and sent for his friends and his wife Zeresh, that he might unburden himself before them, and take counsel with them for Mordochai’s destruction.
entries.cc6e8e5d5861f19ae2395515cedaaba33d9d90cb: <reference osisRef="Esth.5.11-Esth.5.12">Est 5:11-12</reference> <div eID="gen6758" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6759" type="x-p"/> He first spoke to them of his wealth and domestic happiness, of the “glory of his riches and the multitude of his children.” From <reference osisRef="Esth.9.7-Esth.9.10">Est 9:7-10</reference> we learn that Haman had ten sons; and many sons were not looked upon as a great blessing from God by the Israelites only, but were also esteemed a signal prosperity among the Persians, the king annually sending presents to him who had the greatest number of sons.<note placement="foot">Herod. says, i. 136: Ἀνδραγαθίη δ ̓ αὕτη ἀποδέδεκται, μετὰ τὸ μάχεσθαι εἶναι ἀγαθὸν ὅς ἂν πολλοὺς ἀποδέξῃ παῖδας τῷ δὲ τοὺς πλείστους ἀποδεικνύντι δῶρα ἐκπέμπει ὁ βασιλεὺς ἀνὰ πᾶν ἔτος. Comp. Strabo. xv. 3. 17.</note> <div eID="gen6759" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6760" type="x-p"/> Haman next recounted to them the great honours he had attained; כּל־אשׁר את, all how the king had made him great, and how he had advanced him above the princes; comp. Est 3:1. אשׁר is a second accusative of the means by which something is brought to pass. Finally, <reference osisRef="Esth.5.12">Est 5:12</reference>, what high distinction had just been accorded him, by the queen having invited him alone to come to her banquet with the king. “Yea, Esther the queen did let no man come in with the king unto the banquet which she had prepared but myself; and to-morrow am I also invited unto her with the king.” אף enhances the meaning: even this honour is shown me. קרוּא־להּ אני, I am her invited guest = I am invited to her and by her; comp. Ew. §295, <hi type="italic">c</hi>.
entries.383b879266b6f61180c55f8d4cdfb7927a7655cb: <reference osisRef="Esth.5.13">Est 5:13</reference> <div eID="gen6760" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6761" type="x-p"/> And yet all his good fortune is embittered to him as often as he sees the hated Jew Mordochai. “And all this availeth me not at every time when I see the Jew Mordochai sitting in the king’s gate.” לי שׁוה is, not being equalled to me, i.e., not answering my desires, not affording me satisfaction.אשׁר בּכל־עת, at all time when = as often as. The fortune and honour he enjoys fail to satisfy him, when he sees the Jew Mordochai refuse to show him the reverence which he claims.
entries.7db69d76aec9223d3442c88a3ff2a76a49ef083a: <reference osisRef="Esth.5.14">Est 5:14</reference> <div eID="gen6761" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6762" type="x-p"/> His wife and all his friends advise: “Let a tree be made (set up) fifty cubits high, and to-morrow speak to the king, that Mordochai may be hanged thereon (i.e., impaled; see on תּלה <reference osisRef="Esth.2.23">Est 2:23</reference>); and then go in merrily with the king to the banquet.” The counsellors take it for granted that the king will without hesitation agree to Haman’s proposal to execute Mordochai, and therefore advise him at once to make the necessary preparations, so that the hated Jew may be hanged on the morrow before the banquet, and Haman may then go with the king to the feast prepared by the queen, free from all annoyance. גב עץ עשׂה, to make, i.e., to erect a high tree. The higher the stake, the farther would it be seen. The 3rd pers. plur. יעשׂוּ stands instead of the passive: let them make = let ... be made. So too יתלוּ for let ... be hanged. This speech pleased Haman, and he caused the stake to be erected. Elevation of Mordochai and Disgrace of Haman - <reference osisRef="Esth.6.1-Esth.6.14">Est 6:1-14</reference> <div eID="gen6762" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6763" type="x-p"/> The next night the king, being unable to sleep, caused the chronicles of the kingdom to be read to him. The account of the conspiracy discovered by Mordochai, which was written therein, was thus brought before him, and he inquired of his servants whether this man had been rewarded (<hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Esth.6.1-Esth.6.3">Est 6:1-3</reference></hi>). On receiving a negative answer, the king sent to inquire who was in the court; and Haman being found there thus early, he had him summoned, and asked him: what should be done to the man in whose honour the king delighteth. Haman, supposing that the king could intend to honour no one but himself, voted for the very highest public mark of respect (<reference osisRef="Esth.6.3-Esth.6.9">Est 6:3-9</reference>), and was then obliged at the king’s command to pay the proposed honour to Mordochai (<reference osisRef="Esth.6.10">Est 6:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Esth.6.11">Est 6:11</reference>). From this humiliation his wife and friends prognosticated his speedy downfall (<reference osisRef="Esth.6.12-Esth.6.14">Est 6:12-14</reference>).  <chapter eID="Esth.5"/> <div eID="gen6763" type="x-p"/>

entries.cc5bb3733831e6d732d043170ef42f83710dc0ca:
<ns0:div xmlns:ns0="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="5" type="chapter">
                  <ns0:head>CHAP. V.</ns0:head>
                  <ns0:p n="1">1 NOW it came to pass on the third day <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Of which see the notes on <ns0:hi>ch.</ns0:hi> 4. 16.</ns0:note>, that Esther put on <ns0:hi>her</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 6. <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>. & 8. 15.</ns0:note> royal <ns0:hi>apparel</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">That she might ren<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />der her self as amiable in the Kings Eyes as she could; and so ob<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tain her request.</ns0:note>, and stood in the inner court of the kings house, over against the kings house: and the king <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                        <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>at upon his royal throne in the royal house, over against the gate of the house.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="2">2 And it was <ns0:hi>so,</ns0:hi> when the king saw Esther the queen standing in the court, <ns0:hi>that</ns0:hi> she <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 5. <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>. & 7. 3.</ns0:note> obtained favour in his sight: and the king held out to Esther the golden scep<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ter that <ns0:hi>was</ns0:hi> in his hand <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">In testimony that he pardoned her presumption, and accepted her person, and was ready to grant her petition.</ns0:note>. so Esther drew near, and touched the top of the scepter <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">In token of her thankful acceptance of the Kings great favour, and of her re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />verence and submission to his Majesty, whereof that might possi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bly be an usual token, and it may be, at the kings call and invitation to her to come near to him.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="3">3 Then said the king unto her, What wilt thou, queen Esther? and what <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> thy request? <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">See <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> 
                        <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>. 23.</ns0:note> it shall be even given thee to the half of the kingdom.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="4">4 And Esther answered, If <ns0:hi>it seem</ns0:hi> good unto the king, let the king and Haman <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Whom she invited, partly that by shewing such respect to the Kings great favourite, she might insinuate her self into the Kings good opinion and affection; and partly, that if she saw fit, she might then present her request to the King.</ns0:note> come this day unto the banquet that I have prepared for him.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="5">5 Then the king said, Cause Haman to make hast, that he may do as Esther hath said: so the king and Ha<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />man came to the banquet that Esther had prepared.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="6">6 And the king said unto Esther at the banquet of wine <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Either 1. At the latter end of the feast, when they used to drink Wine more freely, whereas in the former part, most of their drink was water. Or, 2. At her banquet; which is so called, because it consisted not of meats, which probably the King had plentifully eaten before at his own Table, but of Fruits and Wines; which banquets were very frequent among the <ns0:hi>Persians.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note>, What is thy petition? and it shall be granted thee: and what <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> thy request? even to the half of the kingdom it shall be performed.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="7">7 Then answered Esther, and said, My petition, and my request <ns0:hi>is;</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="8">8 If I have found favour in the <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                        <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>ight of the king, and if it please the king to grant my petition, and <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Heb. <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>.</ns0:note> to perform my request, let the king and Haman come to the banquet that I shall prepare for them, and I will do to morrow as the king hath said <ns0:hi>g.</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>f</ns0:hi> I will acquaint thee with my humble request. She did not present her petition at this time, but delayed it till the next mee<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ting; either through modesty, or because she was a little daunted with the Kings presence, and had not yet good courage to propose her request: or in policy, because she would further engage the Kings affection to her by a second entertainment, and would also in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />timate to him that her petition was of a more than ordinary na<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ture: and principally by direction and disposition of the divine providence, which took away her courage or utterance for this time that she might have a better opportunity for it the next time by that great accident which happened before it.</ns0:note>
                  </ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="9">
                     <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:379" />9 Then went Haman forth that day, joyful, and with a glad heart: but when Haman saw Mordecai in the kings gate, that he stood not up, nor moved for him <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">Partly lest he should<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>eem, or <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>e interpreted to give him that adoration which he hitherto had justly denied: partly because by his bloody and barbarous design and practise, he had put off all hu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />manity, and forfeited all respect; and partly to shew how little he <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>eared him, and that he had a firm confidence in his God that he would deliver him and his people in this great exigency; which he was the more encouraged to hope, because God had enclined <ns0:hi>Esthers</ns0:hi> heart to that pious & valiant resolution of interceding with the King, which he doubted not would meet with good success.</ns0:note>, he was full of indignation against Mordecai.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="10">10 Nevertheles, Haman refrained himself <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">From taking present vengeance upon <ns0:hi>Mordecai,</ns0:hi> to which he was strongly inclined, & which he might easily have effected either by his own, or any of his servants hands, without any expectation, or fear of inconvenience to himself, who having obtained licence to destroy an whole nation, could easily get a pardon for having killed one obscure and infamous member of it. Herein therefore Gods wise and powerful providence appeared in disposing <ns0:hi>Hamans</ns0:hi> heart, contrary to his own inclination and interest, and making him as it were to put fetters upon his own hands.</ns0:note>, and when he came home, he sent and <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Heb. <ns0:hi>
                           <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                              <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap> 
                           <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                              <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap>.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> called for his friends, and Zeresh his wife.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="11">11 And Haman told them of the glory of his rich<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />es <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">Partly to gratify his own vain-glorious humour: and partly to aggravate <ns0:hi>Mordecai</ns0:hi>'s impudence in denying him civil respect, and to alleviate his own vexation caused by it.</ns0:note>, and the multitude of his children, and all <ns0:hi>the things</ns0:hi> wherein the king had promoted him, and how he had advanced him above the princes & servants of the king.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="12">12 Haman said moreover, Yea, Esther the queen did let no man come in with the king unto the banquet that she had prepared, but my self; and to morrow am I invited unto her also with the king <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">Thus he makes that matter of glorying, which was designed for, and the occasion of his <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> ruine. So ignorant are the wi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sest men<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> and subject to fa<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>al mistakes, rejoycing when they have most cause of fear and grief, and sorrowing for those things which tend to joy and comfort.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="13">13 Yet all this availeth me nothing <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Gives me no content. Such torment did his envy and malice bring upon him.</ns0:note>, so long as I see Mordecai the Jew sitting at the kings gate <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">Enjoying that honour and priviledge without disturbance, and denying me the worship due to me by my place, and by the Kings command: though this last, and the chief cause of his rage, he was somewhat ashamed to express. Either <ns0:hi>Morde<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cai</ns0:hi> was come, having laid by his sackcloth for this time, that he might be in a capacity of coming thither, and so of understanding how matters proceeded. Besides this was a private fast, and so he was not oblig'd alwaies to wear his sackcloth in publick, during the whole time of the fast, though he did once come abroad with it, that the cause of it might be publickly known, and so come to <ns0:hi>Esthers</ns0:hi> ears.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="14">14 Then said Zeresh his wife, and all his friends un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />to him, Let a <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>. <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>.</ns0:note> gallows be made of fifty cubits high <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">That it might be more conspicuous to all, and thereby be more disgraceful to <ns0:hi>Mordecai,</ns0:hi> and strike all <ns0:hi>Hamans</ns0:hi> enemies with the great dread of despising or opposing him.</ns0:note>, and to morrow speak thou unto the king, that Mor<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />decai may be hanged thereon: then go thou in merri<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly with the king unto the banquet. And the thing pleased Haman, and he caused <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 7. 9.</ns0:note> the gallows to be made.</ns0:p>
